paras: The attempted lynching of Isaac Jones took place on the night of January 10, 1903, when a mob of about two hundred people went to the village jail in Tarrytown, New York, intending to hang Jones, a Black man accused of attempting to assault a young white woman. The crowd dispersed after police said Jones had been moved to the county jail, and he was later sentenced to four and a half years in Sing Sing. The mob itself drew only brief notice in the New York press, mentioned in passing in a story about a second accusation against a Black man in the same village.

Jones drove a coal wagon for Dinkel, Jewell & Co. and was married with three children. According to Tarrytown dispatches, he was accused of seizing Mamie Foley, the 21-year-old daughter of Michael Foley of Pocantico Hills, by the throat near the railroad tracks on Cortland street late on the night of January 10 and dragging her toward a shed. Officer Burns heard her screams, chased Jones, and caught him as he was entering a saloon. Jones was held for the grand jury on a charge of attempted assault.

The New-York Tribune reported five days later that on the same Saturday night a mob of two hundred people went to the village jail to lynch Jones. Its members carried clubs and ropes and declared that they would "string up the prisoner to a telegraph pole." The police told the crowd that Jones had been taken to the county jail, a statement the Tribune called "a clever ruse," and the crowd dispersed. No injuries were reported.

Three days later James Hill, a Black man formerly employed by William Rockefeller, was arrested on a charge of attacking Mrs. Louis Wall on Central Avenue, and the Tribune wrote that Tarrytown residents were "aroused" and that "it is feared there will be trouble." No arrests of members of the mob appear in the coverage.
On April 2, 1903, County Judge Platt at White Plains sentenced Jones to four years and six months at hard labor in Sing Sing, telling him, "You are a brute of the worst kind."

The first reports, in the New-York Tribune and The Sun on January 12, appeared under the headlines "Negro Tries Assault" and "Girl Assaulted by Negro" and described the attack as fact, with no mention of a mob. The Tribune added that Jones had been "hurried to White Plains before the crime became generally known." Its account of the mob came only on January 15, inside a story headed "Negro Tries Assault" about the Hill case, where the attempted lynching served as evidence of the town's anger and the police deception was praised as clever.

The Evening World's sentencing report, headlined "Four Years for Negro Brute," identified Jones as the man "nearly lynched in Tarrytown" and gave the woman's name as Annie Foley. None of the white papers criticized the mob, and no Black newspaper account of the attempt appears in the coverage.

The Tribune's two stories differ on where Jones was when the mob arrived: the first said he had been hurried to White Plains, while the second called the police statement that he had gone to the county jail a ruse. The woman is named Mamie Foley in both January dispatches and Annie Foley in the April sentencing report.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Isaac Jones
bases: A mob of about two hundred armed with clubs and ropes went to the village jail to hang a Black prisoner and dispersed without reaching him (A4), an episode the Evening World later called a near-lynching (A7).

A mob of two hundred acting on an accusation of attempted assault sought to hang Jones without legal authority (A4), but no one was killed: the crowd dispersed and Jones was later tried and sentenced (A4, A7); this was an attempted lynching.

The accusation and arrest are reported independently by the Tribune and the Sun (A2, A3); the mob at the jail is described only by the Tribune (A4), but the Evening World independently refers to Jones as 'nearly lynched in Tarrytown' (A7).

accounts.label: Tarrytown dispatches on the arrest
accounts.gist: Jones seized Mamie Foley near the railroad tracks, Officer Burns caught him after a chase, and he was held for the grand jury; the Tribune added that he was hurried to White Plains before the crime became generally known. Neither mentions a mob.

accounts.label: Tribune follow-up
accounts.gist: On the Saturday night a mob of two hundred with clubs and ropes went to the village jail to hang Jones; police said he had been taken to the county jail, which the paper called a ruse, and the crowd dispersed.

accounts.label: White Plains sentencing report
accounts.gist: Jones, 'nearly lynched in Tarrytown', was sentenced to four and a half years in Sing Sing, the judge calling him 'a brute of the worst kind'.

framing.detail: The Tribune and Sun ran the arrest as 'Negro Tries Assault' and 'Girl Assaulted by Negro', stating the attack as fact rather than allegation and not mentioning a mob.
The Tribune's later story reported the mob without condemnation, called the police deception 'a clever ruse', and framed the town as justly 'aroused' by attacks of 'several negroes'.
The Evening World headlined the sentencing 'Four Years for Negro Brute' and mentioned the near-lynching only as an identifying detail.

conflicts.note: Both are Tribune reports; the 'ruse' wording implies the police statement was untrue, while the earlier story says he had in fact been moved. The coverage does not settle where he was when the mob arrived.
The two contemporaneous Tarrytown reports agree on Mamie; the Evening World sentencing note is later and brief.
